state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: The correct rule to follow when adding two odd numbers is to recognize that the sum will always be an even number. In your calculation, you correctly added the numbers together, but you incorrectly concluded that the result was odd. Remember, 2n represents an even number, so the sum of two odd numbers will always be even.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Turn 2 (student): Okay, I think I get that 2n is supposed to be even, but I'm still confused about how adding the odd number \(2m + 1\) changes things. So, if I add two odd numbers, like 3 and 5, how does that fit into this? Does it still end up being even?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: When adding two odd numbers, such as 3 and 5, you will always get an even number as the sum. Remember, an odd number plus another odd number will result in an even number because the sum of two odd numbers is always even. Keep practicing and you will start to see this pattern more clearly.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I see what you're saying about the sum of two odd numbers being even. So, when I add 3 and 5, I get 8, which is even. But I'm still not sure how that connects with the \(2n\) part. Can you explain again why \(2n\) is always even?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher repeatedly states facts without engaging the student's specific confusion about why 2n represents an even number, provides no reasoning opportunities, and the student ends still asking the same fundamental question about 2n being even.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to state rules about odd and even numbers, they fail to show worked algebraic steps, don't provide explicit procedures for the proof structure, and give vague corrective feedback rather than directly addressing the student's procedural error of writing 2n+(2m+1) instead of (2n+1)+(2m+1).
